title: Burnham 'open' to calls for slavery apology but rules out reparations
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he is "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, but has
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he is "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, but has ruled out financial reparations.He said he wanted a "dialogue with those affected" and was open to "calls for an apology", but said reparations were "not the right answer".The statement was welcomed by the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) for Afrikan Reparations, with its chairwoman Bell Ribeiro-Adday telling BBC Radio 4's Today programme the issue was not just about money.It comes ahead of next week's Commonwealth leaders summit in the Caribbean. As King Charles III tours the region, there have been renewed calls for an apology.During the first leg of his tour in the Bahamas, the King made reference to the "suffering of the past". Later, in Guyana, he visited the site of a rebellion of enslaved people against British authorities. On Saturday, Burnham described the transatlantic slave trade, when Africans were trafficked to the Americas, as a "brutal and barbaric violation" and said Britain must "face up to the past".The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations. Burnham has stuck with the policy of his predecessors, and has stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments. "I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part," Burnham wrote in a piece for the Guardian, external.He said Commonwealth countries had for years been asking for an "honest conversation". He said he wanted to offer a "structured dialogue", adding: "Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process. I am open to them."Chancellor John Healey told the BBC that Burnham was "open to a discussion" about an apology because it was "the right thing, particularly ahead of the Commonwealth heads conference". The Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting starts on 1 November in Antigua, and will be opened by the King as part of his tour. Speaking to Laura Kuenssberg, Healey said the prime minister does not think reparations are the right approach.He added that a formal apology doesn't mean British people should now "accept the financial liability for any part in things that happened hundreds of years ago in which they had no role".Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said there was "no reason British taxpayers today should be held financially responsible for things that happened generations before any of us were born."In a post on X, Badenoch wrote that Labour was "already spending too much on Britain's welfare state, now is not the time for Andy Burnham to be providing global welfare."Bell Ribeiro-Addy said that while her parliamentary group welcomed the government's acceptance of the role it played, it had "still fallen short of a formal state apology and that actually costs nothing"."Acknowledgement is not the same as understanding," she told Today, adding: "Until we apologise, we are never going to be on equal footing… it's meant to be a family of nations - a Commonwealth - and it's simply not the case."Ribeiro-Addy, who is MP for Clapham and Brixton Hill, said that, to her knowledge, an invoice for financial reparations has not been given to the UK, and so discussing "reparative justice" on those ends, was missing the point."My worry is the focus on financial reparations, and I think that is deeply problematic and has not quite listened to what people have said," Ribeiro-Addy said.Downing Street believes it is in the UK's interest to strengthen the Commonwealth, in a world where China and Russia are seeking to exert influence.Only this week, President Vladimir Putin hosted a Russia-Africa summit in Moscow. Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley, who has sought reparations, welcomed Burnham's statement, saying she would engage in good faith while still seeking reparatory justice.Denis O'Brien, founder of The Repair Campaign, said Burnham's statement was disappointing and did not go far enough."The British government must stop obfuscating and give a full and formal apology now," he said. "This would be a significant and symbolic first step towards reparatory justice." From the 16th Century, English authorities and the monarchy were prominent participants in the centuries-long slave trade.In 2007, the then Prime Minister Tony Blair said the UK's role in the slave trade was a matter of "deep sorrow and regret".Britain had a key role in ending the trade, through Parliament's passage of a law to abolish slavery in 1833.As part of that law, British plantation owners were paid for the loss of people they had enslaved.The UK only finished paying off the debt it incurred to cover the payments in 2015.

schema.headline: Burnham 'open' to calls for slavery apology but rules out reparations

title: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
description: In an update on Saturday morning, Zelensky said around 200,000 households in the Dnipro region were left without electricity as well as at least 80,00
body: In an update on Saturday morning, Zelensky said around 200,000 households in the Dnipro region were left without electricity as well as at least 80,000 households in the Kyiv region following Russian strikes on Friday night.He accused Russia of "deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure every day".The US approved sale of Patriot missiles comes after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump earlier this month when the US eased sanctions on Russia as part of a deal to secure Russian diesel. The US president stated it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader to strike a deal to end the war with Russia. Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, having earlier seized Crimea and parts of Donbas in the east. Tensions eased after Zelensky held talks with US envoys in Oslo on 20 October.In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe".It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan". The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale".Meanwhile, at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting European diplomats protested over the presence of Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov by refusing to stand for an official photograph.The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio."Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Lavrov at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine.

schema.headline: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine

title: Spain train disaster clouds Pedro Sánchez chances of re-election
description: The formal investigation into the Toledo train disaster has only just been launched but the government has been quick to take control of the narrative
body: The formal investigation into the Toledo train disaster has only just been launched but the government has been quick to take control of the narrative.From the first hours after the collision, Transport Minister Oscar Puente began suggesting "human error" was to blame, batting responsibility as far as possible from the cabinet.On Friday, he appeared before the press for a second time to set out what he called the "objective facts" of the crash and counter a surge of criticism against the government.The opposition People's Party (PP) is among those calling for his resignation as a "moral" and "ethical" move.Instead after expressing "huge pain and sadness" for the victims, Puente went on the offensive.He rejected talk of chronic underinvestment in infrastructure and insisted that Spain's high-speed signalling safety system, the LZB, was neither old nor inadequate: Germany and Austria use the same.In Spain, it has already failed 170 times so far this year, he revealed, but called that "normal" and around the EU average.The problem surrounds what happens next - when the system fails and control of the line shifts to manual.In this case, the minister highlighted a series of human errors that proved catastrophic.Crucially, at one point a controller instructed a stalled train to restart, clearing it to advance at up to 160km/h (100 mph) even though a second train was stuck on the line up ahead.The impending collision was clear from audio calls and on big screens in the control centre in Madrid."They worked. We checked. They could see what was happening," Puente confirmed. But the advancing train was never ordered to stop."I'm no judge... But these are the facts."So would he take personal and political responsibility anyway, and resign? Puente called it his "duty", rather, to remain as minister."I'll face up to things, explain, elucidate," he countered. "I'll think how to improve the system, and give confidence to those who want to travel by train and feel calm and safe."But Spaniards will take a lot of persuading."This is not only a very serious accident, but the second in a very short time," Paco Camas of the pollster Ipsos points out.An investigation into January's crash in Adamuz, near Cordoba, is still open, with initial reports suggesting there was a crack in the rails -  very different to the latest collision.But there is a similar impact."It destroys people's confidence not only in the railways but institutions in general," Camas warns. "And in Spain when such things happen, we know that people blame their government."For Team Sánchez it is the latest in a spiral of crises.Allegations of corruption against the prime minister's close relatives still persist, all denied.Then there was a sudden influx of migrants from Morocco this summer to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. That got right-wing opponents shouting about incompetence and underfunding.Later, a video of a pensioner being forcibly evicted from her home went viral and sparked street protests.That's when Sánchez called an early election.His chances of winning the vote looked slim even before the train crash. Now they have plummeted.Most recent polls showed the centre-right PP coming first and forming a coalition with the far-right Vox."They have this majority in almost 95% of the simulations we have done," Prof Pablo Simon of Madrid's Carlos III University explains.But Sánchez had been running a positive campaign, trying to lure apathetic voters to the polls to vote socialist.Suddenly, the tone has changed."They've totally lost control of the agenda and the emotion of this campaign," Simon says. "It's going to be extremely difficult now. There is this general mood of decay, of a country that's not working properly. A depression."There is also anger.There have already been small protests over the train crash led by far-right groups in Madrid and large numbers of police are on stand-by this weekend ahead of further potential clashes, organised online.Here in Toledo, the mood is nervous."We all travelled in silence and really sad," Paloma told me at the city station, where she had just pulled in on a half empty train.She admitted she's scared of the high-speed network now and angry at the government."This crash will change all of our votes, completely," Paloma said. "We'll shift from the left wing to the right. Because of everything that's happened."Lucia takes the high-speed AVE into Madrid each day, and is scared too."This was human error. But there's been two accidents now with more than 100 dead," she says. "Things here are really bad. They have to change."Producer Davide Ghiglione contributed to this report

schema.headline: Spain train disaster clouds Pedro Sánchez chances of re-election

title: Ukrainian evacuees reunite with family after years trapped in Russia-occupied city
description: There were raw emotional scenes as people evacuated from the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky crossed from Belarus into the Ukrainian regio
body: There were raw emotional scenes as people evacuated from the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky crossed from Belarus into the Ukrainian region of Chernihiv.Families cried as they reunited with relatives they had not seen for years, with two sisters running and crying out as they embraced their father.Some elderly residents were so weak they were carried on stretchers. They had been trapped in the frontline city without food, water and electricity, with many resorting to cooking garden weeds to survive. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky thanked US First Lady Melania Trump for her efforts in brokering a local ceasefire that paved the way for their evacuation on Friday.Upon their arrival, Dasha and Anya Palii sprinted across the tarmac screaming towards the bus carrying their father Mykhailo.Their cries and their tears captured the sheer relief of three years of desperate worry, fearing they would never see him again.Their mother Zhanna clasped Mykhailo's face and stroked his forehead again and again, as if checking he was the same man she had left behind. He promised her, finally, they will now get married.Tetiana and Volodymyr, an older couple carrying their cat, told the BBC they no longer have a home, after it was burned down in the first year of the war. They have been living in the abandoned house of a neighbour. They said they instantly took the decision to leave but feared their journey could be disrupted. Now they have to work out where to go next and how to rebuild their lives.The ceasefire allowed the road out of the city to be cleared of mines and humanitarian aid to be delivered.Ceasefire measures will remain in place until the end of Sunday 1 November.Residents had a four-hour window to leave before a convoy of 25 buses, with space for 750 people, left the town on Friday afternoon - along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay in the war-torn city, despite widespread devastation and the lack of gas, electricity and running water.Some of the older generation did not want to leave, one relative told the BBC.Lubinets said on Friday morning that those who decided to stay "will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance".He and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova travelled to Oleshky together on Friday, setting off from Armiansk, in the Russian-occupied Crimean peninsula.Lubinets is the first Ukrainian official since the start of the war to visit Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.Zelensky praised him and his team for helping move evacuees out to safety.The Ukrainian president also thanked those who had helped bring attention to the "true humanitarian catastrophe in Ukrainian territory temporarily occupied by Russia".The ceasefire has required close cooperation between Lubinets and Lantratova, which Lubinets said he carried out in the interests of saving lives.But some in Ukraine have recoiled at the sight of him standing beside a representative of the Russian occupying power which has killed so many of the city's residents and made life unbearable for the rest.Russia said on Thursday that it had prepared "dozens of tonnes" of aid for the residents who do not wish to leave, including food, medicine, hygiene products and fuel for generators.Additional reporting by George Wright

schema.headline: Ukrainian evacuees reunite with family after years trapped in Russia-occupied city

title: The fight to save Canadian town threatened by Trump's tariffs
description: Figure caption, "We're going to fight" - How a paper mill's uncertain future could devastate tiny Quebec townByJessica MurphyCanada digital editor and
body: Figure caption, "We're going to fight" - How a paper mill's uncertain future could devastate tiny Quebec townByJessica MurphyCanada digital editor and Nadine YousifSenior Canada reporterAs you cross the Ottawa river into Témiscaming, Quebec, the paper mill takes up much of the horizon.The town itself was built over a century ago, around the mill and the region's forests  filled with pine, birch, spruce and fir. Now, the main employer and economic anchor sits idle after trade talks broke down between Canada and the US and President Donald Trump imposed more tariffs on the country.Most of the mill‘s 360 employees are out of work, kept afloat for the moment with partial pay from government tariff-relief. For some, like Nadine Suley, the shuttering of the mill could mark not just a lost livelihood, but a lost way of life. She is not "a city girl", and is heading out moose hunting later to take advantage of the short season, like much of the town. She quips they'll all need the free meat provided by the animals this year. "It's not just a job. It's our home," Suley says, adding that the US tariffs on her town feel like "a personal attack". In early October, American owner RYAM went ahead with an "economic shutdown" of the mill for "an indefinite period". Property values in Témiscaming fell almost overnight, and "For Sale" signs dot the yards of modest middle-class homes that make up most of the town. There are fears that essential service people - from grocery store clerks to the doctors at the small local hospital - could also be on their way out."If the mill goes down, it'll turn into a ghost town," says Ronnie Raymond, who like many in the town comes from a family of mill workers. "There'll be nothing, nothing left. There's no work for anybody, really. It's scary."Image source, BBC/Jessica MurphyImage caption, The paper mill has served as the economic engine of Témiscaming for over a century.At a high level, Canada's economy has weathered the ongoing trade war with the US, its largest customer. The national unemployment rate has remained largely steady at around 6.5% since Trump's tariffs were first implemented. It's been coupled with tepid but consistent economic growth.But a closer look at the numbers shows pockets of deep pain in industries directly hit by US tariffs of up to 50%, like steel, aluminium, automobiles and - in the case of  Témiscaming - lumber, pulp and paper. It raises questions about whether the Carney government is doing enough to help those struggling while a trade deal remains elusive."If there was 10% of job loss in Toronto or Montreal or Quebec City or Vancouver, it'd be all over the news, and it'd be a lot of pressure on the governments to do something,” says Stéphane Lefebvre, an employee and union leader, whose father and grandfather also worked at the mill. That economic pain could have ripple effects on the entire forestry industry in the region, including saw mills and trucking. One local contractor told the BBC he has already had to lay off 13 people.The last time the town faced a threat this existential was in 1973, when the mill's then-American owner threatened to shut it down, prompting the local workers and managers to come together and purchase it.They turned it into Tembec, a Quebec-owned, international company with branches across North America and France. The workers now hope to do it again, mobilising a coalition of locals who want to buy the plant back from RYAM, which purchased it in 2017. "We're hoping that lightning will hit twice," Lefebvre says, speaking inside the town's union hall.But he contends that they cannot do so without significant help from Prime Minister Mark Carney and the Quebec government, either in the form of tariff relief or financial support. Suley notes that the prime minister has placed emphasis on "buy local" and supporting Canadian workers since he was elected. Backing the town's bid to buy back the mill, she says, would be a way for Carney to fulfil that pledge. In an email to the BBC, RYAM said it would not comment on a potential sale of the plant or any prospective buyers.Image source, BBC/Nadine YousifImage caption, Stéphane Lefebvre, his father and grandfather all worked at the paper mill in Témiscaming.Mayor Alain Gauthier doesn't blame RYAM for its decision. He calls US tariffs "a bomb to shut down our manufacturing in Canada". He wants Ottawa to retaliate with its own duties on the board products coming into Canada from the US, currently tariff-free.And he says that while politicians have said Canada is in an economic war with the US, "in reality we see absolutely no evidence of war measures being taken". "We feel we got into a war with kid's water guns to fight back." Some, like Lefebvre, feel that forestry has taken a back seat in the fight to save other tariffed industries like steel and autos.This month, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly threatened Stelco - one of Canada's largest steelmakers - with financial penalties or a forced asset sale should they go ahead with the planned layoffs of some 500 workers due to steel tariffs pressure. Stelco in Hamilton, near Toronto, is owned by US-based Cleveland-Cliffs, which committed to keeping jobs in Canada when it bought the firm in 2024. Last week, Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford announced nearly C$9bn ($6.4bn; £4.8bn) to help Ontario's steel and auto sector. The funds will be used to help the industries modernise, strengthen domestic demand and open new markets overseas, they said.Sébastien Lemire, the elected MP for Témiscaming from the Bloc Québécois party, told the BBC that he is "very concerned and worried" about what he calls inaction from the Carney government to support the town and Quebec's forestry industry more broadly.A spokesperson for Minister Joly told the BBC in a statement that the government has made available $400m to support the forestry sector in rural and remote areas.It has also launched a programme to help businesses impacted by tariffs to access cash-flow while they work to pivot away from US markets. On the Témiscaming mill, the spokesperson said that the government "is actively working with all parties involved to find a viable solution to the issues facing the company, while responsibly managing Canadians' dollars."Image source, Supplied/Stéphane LefebvreImage caption, Témiscaming residents gathered for a Union-led rally to support the mill's workers and draw attention to the woes of the lumber industry. In August, after the breakdown in trade talks, the US imposed 50% duties on a some C$28bn of Canadian goods, including wood and paper products like pulp, stationery and boxes. Canada in response imposed its own "dollar-for-dollar" counter-tariffs. The Témiscaming mill, which produces paperboard used in frozen-food packaging across North America and in the scratch-off lottery tickets commonly found at convenience stores, sends roughly 75% of its production to the US.Trump argues these import taxes boost US manufacturing and create jobs - essentially seeking to protect US workers who could face similar fates to those in Témiscaming. Frank Dottori has been through all of this before. Now in his 80s and retired in Témiscaming, he was an engineer at the mill that was instrumental in organising its employees in the 1970s to take a 10% cut in order to collectively purchase it. He went on to become CEO.Their ambitions were seen as foolish at the time, and he recalls being "politely ejected" by the Quebec premier when he first came knocking for support. But they prevailed with the help of the labour union and an ex-employee with executive experience and plenty of swagger. Dottori attributes their success to this person's forceful charisma.Dottori said the new generation of workers need someone just as bold."Does the local group have that? Highly unlikely. Can they get it? Yeah, if they organise themselves," he said. Image source, BBC/Nadine YousifImage caption, Frank Dottori led the effort to buy the Témiscaming mill in the 1970s during a period of economic hardship It is also imperative, he says, that US tariffs be lifted to restore the mill's long-term economic viability, at least in the short term.Many workers in Témiscaming say they are placing some hope in the upcoming US midterm elections to put pressure on Trump — whose approval ratings have fallen among Americans, according to polls — to ease some of his tariffs on Canada."We'll take any help we can get," Suley says, adding: "There are Americans that care what's going on, and it's affecting them too."There are signs the Trump administration is taking note of that pressure, with some tariffs on Canadian goods lifted last week after lobbying from Republican Maine Senator Susan Collins, who is running for re-election in November. Those changes don't apply to products made at Témiscaming's mill, however.Suley and others hope a resolution will come quickly, before winter, when sub-zero temperatures could freeze equipment at the idle plant, causing damage that would make reopening even more difficult.In the meantime, Lefebvre says he is committed to making the dream of local ownership of the mill a reality, regardless of what happens."We're in Game Seven right now," he says. "We're gonna play till the last whistle."

schema.headline: The fight to save Canadian town threatened by Trump's tariffs

title: How to prepare for an emergency: What households in different countries stock up on
description: Dan C, a physiotherapist in Maryland, started his emergency supply after becoming a father. So far, he has spent about $6,000 (£4,470), storing it on
body: Dan C, a physiotherapist in Maryland, started his emergency supply after becoming a father. So far, he has spent about $6,000 (£4,470), storing it on shelves in his basement."It's part of my responsibility as a parent," says Dan, 38, who has two children under 10.A few years ago his house was cut off during a "very cold" February and the family was without power for two days. Though he'd already started keeping supplies, "there were numerous gaps in what I had prepared for," he says.Dan's stash now includes 150 gallons of water and several large water storage containers made of soft plastic, which can be filled and kept in the bath. He also keeps things like chlorine dioxide tablets, which are often used to make water from streams or rivers safe to drink.His "rotating pantry" - consisting of long-life food supplies like oats, quinoa and peanut butter - is regularly used for cooking then replaced so "it's not just sitting there expiring". For his family-of-four, he has about three months of food supplies.Dan also has solar panels, a camping stove, a tent, wood supplies and a propane fireplace insert that can run off grid - without electricity or wood. He also keeps extensive medical supplies - including bleeding control kits.In the US, the Federal Emergency Management Agency, external advises people to assemble an emergency kit, make a family emergency plan, and be informed about how to respond to different incidents.Dan says when it comes to emergency planning, "there can be a tendency to catastrophise," but for him, it's about being a "responsible homeowner".Ayumi T, who lives in Tokyo, has kept an emergency bag for years in case of events like earthquakes, typhoons and extreme heat. But after an earthquake in 2024 killed hundreds of people and caused widespread damage to Japan's Noto Peninsula, Ayumi stocked up even more.Tokyo's government has a 68-page disaster prevention guide, external, which details what to keep in an emergency kit and what to do in certain emergency situations.In her emergency rucksack - kept in her wardrobe - Ayumi keeps clothes, towels, menstrual products, disposable chopsticks, sticky notes, disposable masks and a disposable toilet, like those used by hikers and campers."A lot of it is old stuff I don't use anymore," Ayumi, 27, who works at a university, says.Every new year, her family check their kits and update them if necessary, replacing out-of-date food, for example.Over the past five years, "it's been on my mind, 'what happens in case of emergency?'", Nicole Bonds says.The leadership coach in Atlanta, puts this down to noticing "significantly more and more" severe weather patterns and storms around the world and a lack of preparedness.Her motto is "don't panic, be prepared", she says.As well as a large selection of cleaning and hygiene products, Nicole, 48, has bought batteries, a power bank, first-aid supplies, rechargeable fans, blankets and sleeping bags.To keep it affordable she picks up a small amount of supplies "here and there" to gradually build up her stock. She keeps some of the items under her bed, in packing bags and in her kitchen cabinets.Where Michael Stuut lives in the Netherlands is below sea level. He says he worries about extreme weather but also possible war.The 39-year-old, who lives in Hoorn with his wife and five-year-old son, started preparing his kit a few years ago.Michael keeps a healthy stash of power equipment as well as food - including a Starlink Mini, a small and lightweight satellite device for internet access.He keeps supplies in his attic and a crawl space under the house - here lies about 120 litres of water, cash, a first-aid kit and a generator.Earlier this year, Michael created an app to log his food supplies and when they might expire."Being prepared isn't about panic," he says. "It's about being the calm one when the lights go out."In late 2025, Dutch authorities launched a campaign that instructed households to have 72 hours' worth of supplies, much like UK authorities have just done.At the beginning of his prepping journey, Michael's wife didn't see the need, but he says she now understands the importance. They've told their five-year-old the supplies are simply for when they don't want to go to the shop, adding they "don't want to burden him".Michael is sceptical of the three-day advice - also recommended by the UK - but says: "Every household that has a few basic things at home makes it easier for the emergency services to help the people who need it most."Additional reporting by Hanae Takahashi and Richard Frost

schema.headline: How to prepare for an emergency: What households in different countries stock up on

title: Jamie Carragher apologises to Aston Villa for 'wrong' language
description: Jamie Carragher has apologised to Aston Villa, the club's owners and their fans for using "clumsy and wrong" language when linking manager Unai Emery
body: Jamie Carragher has apologised to Aston Villa, the club's owners and their fans for using "clumsy and wrong" language when linking manager Unai Emery with becoming Manchester United head coach.On Friday, Villa said they would initiate legal action against the former England defender for what they described as "unacceptable insults".The club's statement, signed by chairman Nassef Sawiris, referred to comments made by Carragher on the Stick to Football podcast, when he suggested Emery would want to manage a "giant" club.He also told the club's fans to shut up, adding: "Aston Villa will never be Manchester United."Posting on social media on Saturday, Carragher said his comments were intended to be "tongue in cheek"."I'd like to apologise to Aston Villa, the owners and their fans," the pundit wrote."My language this week was clumsy and wrong."I can assure Villa fans it was tongue in cheek but I can understand it's not come across that way, so apologies."Manchester United manager Michael Carrick's position is hanging in the balance following a dismal start to the season.Referring to former Paris St-Germain and Arsenal boss Emery, Carragher said on Stick to Football: "Surely he would want that opportunity to manage a giant again."There is a chain in football, whether you like it or not."So Real Madrid will take Manchester United's best player, they did it with [Cristiano] Ronaldo. And there will be teams below Aston Villa, and they'll take their players or manager, so shut the [expletive] up Aston Villa fans. Aston Villa will never be Manchester United."After his comments attracted criticism from Villa fans, Carragher responded on social media, stating that telling them to shut up had been "a joke" and he had been praising Emery and the club "for years".He reiterated on the Overlap Daily podcast that his message to Villa fans had been meant "in jest", adding: "I just think Unai Emery is the best manager in the league and if you're Man Utd you're thinking, what's the best we can get?"

schema.headline: Jamie Carragher apologises to Aston Villa for 'wrong' language

title: Celebrity Traitors comes to a climax in nail-biting final
description: Image source, BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan CherryImage caption, Seven celebrities remained at the start of the final episodeByIan YoungsCulture reporterUpd
body: Image source, BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan CherryImage caption, Seven celebrities remained at the start of the final episodeByIan YoungsCulture reporterUpdated 5 hours agoSpoiler warning: This story reveals details of The Celebrity Traitors finalWe've had four weeks of suspense, suspicion and very suspect tactics, as some of Britain's biggest stars engaged in a battle of wits to win the most popular show on TV.The second series of BBC One's The Celebrity Traitors reached its climax on Friday, with the 21 original contestants having been reduced to seven before the final.They were then whittled down to two winners - with the faithful duo of comedian Romesh Ranganathan and Heartstopper actor Sebastian "Bash" Croft emerging victorious.The players successfully banished the remaining traitors - Love Island host Maya Jama and YouTuber King Kenny - in dramatic fashion, and the winning pair shared the £83,000 prize for their charities.Image source, Paul Chappells/ Studio Lambert/BBCImage caption, Romesh Ranganathan and Sebastian "Bash" Croft celebrated with host Claudia WinklemanFigure caption, What just happened in Celebrity Traitors final?As it happened: Relive the Celebrity Traitors finalWatch The Celebrity Traitors on BBC iPlayerGet all the reaction on Uncloaked on BBC iPlayerThe finale drew an average audience of 11.2 million live viewers, and that number will rise when catch-up is included. Other recent episodes have been watched by more than 15 million, including catch-up.Kenny reached the final stage, the endgame, after turning on his fellow traitor Maya at the last round table.Kenny, Romesh and Bash were joined by singer James Blunt in the climax of the endgame, where the remaining contestants gather around a fire pit to decide whether they think there are any traitors left.When James and Kenny were tied in a vote for who was a traitor, Bash persuaded Romesh to banish Kenny instead of James - thereby securing victory for team faithful."Absolutely devastated. Almost scraped it," Kenny seethed. "I was so close, I smelled the victory." However, he can take consolation from the fact his performance on the show has established him as a mainstream star.Figure caption, The final reveal of the Celebrity TraitorsIn a further twist, James chose another round of voting and was subsequently evicted himself, leaving Romesh and Bash as the last men standing."This might actually be the best day of my life," said 24-year-old Bash through tears of joy.He, too, can expect a major career boost.Romesh reflected: "I just really hope my mum's proud. And also my youngest son Charlie, who wanted me to come on the show - dad won. Please show me some respect."The pair will split their winnings between two refugee charities, the Refugee Council and Choose Love.Image source, Euan Cherry/Studio Lambert/BBCImage caption, Traitors Kenny and Maya fell at the final hurdleImage source, BBC/Studio Lambert/Paul ChappellsImage caption, The final six: Maya, James, Kenny, Romesh, Leigh-Anne and BashEarlier, actor Michael Sheen was murdered in the first action of Friday's episode. "I am incredibly disappointed," he said. "Gutted that I got so close to the end. It's been absolutely unforgettable."When it came to the endgame, Little Mix singer Leigh-Anne Pinnock was swiftly banished after Kenny voted to remove her."I was thinking me and him had a mutual understanding, and now I feel so stupid," she raged."But I'm walking away feeling super proud and like I've really accomplished something here."Image source, BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan CherryImage caption, James Blunt helped retrieve the final prize money in a mission involving dynamite and helicoptersMeanwhile, James B was left rueing one final mistake in a long but valiant catalogue of misjudgements throughout the series.The singer, who looked aghast when he was attacked by Romesh during the endgame, was then the only one to choose to banish again when it came to the final three.James was unaware that Romesh and Bash had both chosen to end the game - meaning he too could have been a winner if he had done the same - but became the victim of his own choice to banish."I've loved trying to work it out, I've loved getting it wrong so often, I've loved the tiny moments when I've got it right," he said wistfully. "I've loved the game."Image source, Euan Cherry/Studio Lambert/BBCImage caption, James Acaster effectively banished himself in a novel twist in the showCelebrities who departed earlier in the series included ex-EastEnders actor Ross Kemp, model Jerry Hall, sitcom star Miranda Hart, comedian Joe Lycett, presenter Hannah Fry and former BBC journalist Amol Rajan.This series is also likely to be remembered for the two contestants who made the unorthodox decision to reveal themselves as traitors, before being summarily dispatched by their fellow players.First, actor Richard E Grant was so giddy to have received the tap on the shoulder that he blurted out his supposedly secret status in episode two.Comedian James Acaster, meanwhile, was the most reluctant traitor in the history of The Traitors, and unexpectedly gave himself up when he came under pressure at the round table in Thursday's penultimate episode.Aftermath of Acaster's admission There have been reports, external that filming of the scene was paused and he was checked by welfare staff after he became anxious.Asked about the reports, a BBC spokesperson said on Friday that the safety and welfare of those taking part was the "highest priority", and "players are closely monitored and supported throughout by production which includes a dedicated and experienced welfare team".Speculation about the round table being heavily edited was fuelled when eagle-eyed viewers noticed, external a shot of Romesh reacting in shock - apparently to James A's initial confession - which in fact seemed to have come from a later moment, after Romesh had voted for James by writing his name on the blackboard.In the episode, the sequence where the celebrities all voted for James in light of his admission was shown as a relatively quick and straightforward process, raising a question about what prompted Romesh's shocked look.Acaster did not take part in Friday's edition of spin-off show Uncloaked, which reunited some of the celebrity contestants following the final.'A bit dull?'The comedian's bombshell the previous night did provide the programme with a twist to spark it to life after what some viewers saw as a mid-series lull.On Thursday, the Hollywood Reporter noted, external that the show had achieved record-breaking ratings - before asking: "Why, then, has much of the consensus on social media been that it's all felt a bit dull?"Some noted a shortage of true back-stabbing, double-crossing and explosive rows - the things, in other words, that viewers love the most - while the celebrities were more chummy and savvy than previous groups of castle dwellers.And while there was no shortage of big characters, this season lacked an equivalent to Alan Carr, the hugely popular and apparently hapless comedian who lied and murdered his way to an unlikely victory as a traitor last year.The drama ramped up in the final, though, and Friday's episode is likely to have been the most watched TV programme of the year.

schema.headline: Celebrity Traitors comes to a climax in nail-biting final

title: The Stroud woman whose short story inspired Hollywood film Wicker
description: Author's camping trip inspired Hollywood film WickerImage source, Black BearImage caption, The film Wicker, which opens in UK cinemas on 30 October, w
body: Author's camping trip inspired Hollywood film WickerImage source, Black BearImage caption, The film Wicker, which opens in UK cinemas on 30 October, was based on Ursula Wills' short storyBySacha BigwoodReporting fromGloucestershireAn author who was inspired to write a short story after seeing wicker sculptures on a camping trip has said she never imagined it would become a raunchy A-list feature film.Ursula Wills from Stroud, in Gloucestershire, had just returned from a holiday in Cornwall in 2006 when she wrote The Wicker Husband, which follows an ostracised fisherwoman who pays a basket-maker to weave her a husband.The story was picked up by writers who "livened it up" for the big screen to become Wicker, starring Olivia Colman, Alexander Skarsgård and Peter Dinklage.Wills called it a "unique and amazing" film that she thinks "audiences are going to go crazy for".The author, who completed a Master of Arts degree at Bath Spa University in 2004, and spent 19 years living in Bristol, drew inspiration for the 14-page story on a camping trip."I'd visited this place called Melinsey Mill, which is an old watermill, where a basket maker had created an art trail around the pond, with big wicker sculptures like a stag, a giant spider, and a wicker man fishing, and I thought what would anyone want a wicker man for?" she said."I had the idea for the story straight away."Figure caption, Author Ursula Wills speaks to BBC Local Radio. Picture: Black BearWills posted The Wicker Husband on a short story website called East of the Web. After racking up interest from readers, she was contacted by actor Rhys Jennings who, alongside Olivier Award–winning composer Darren Clark, created a musical.In March 2020, it opened at Watermill Theatre in Newbury, but after only four nights the theatre had to close because of the Covid-19 pandemic.Image source, Mark Dawson PhotographyImage caption, Ursula Wills is the author of the short story, 'The Wicker Husband' which has been transformed into a feature filmA year later, she was approached by producer Justin Lothrop who asked her for film rights."I had a meeting with writers and directors, but after Olivia Colman came onboard in 2023 things rolled out really fast," Wills said."By the end of 2024 I was out in Budapest where the film was being shot."When I read the script, I thought it was going to be good, and when I saw it being shot in Hungary I knew it - the end result is something unique and amazing. "I think audiences are going to go crazy for it."Image source, Tor Books UKImage caption, Ursula Wills' story has been translated into German and ItalianWicker, which opens in UK cinemas on 30 October and has been described as a raunchy fantasy rom-com, has garnered lots of attention online and spawned countless viral posts.Although Wills has said the finished film remains faithful to her original short story, the intimate relationship between the fisherwoman and her wicker husband has been embellished to "liven it up".Joint writer-directors Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson said they "loved it immediately". "It was very sort of sparsely written, but just had these beautiful little clues throughout that suggested to us what the tone of the film could become," they explained."We realised this was more than a period fable. We immediately saw a satirical comedy about sex and marriage, a unique visual spectacle, and a strange love story that would ground it all."Image source, Black BearImage caption, Peter Dinklage's character was inspired by the art trail at Melinsey MillThe UK premiere for the film was held earlier this month at the British Film Institute in London. For Wills it was not all glamourous."I had to scuttle away from the afterparty at 21:45 to get the train back to Swindon and then I had to get a rail replacement bus to Stroud," she said.Wills now has a literary agent, and has a new collection of 13 short stories coming out across the world in April.However, she explained the journey of The Wicker Husband was not over yet."I wouldn't have predicted that it was going to be a full film with an A-list cast, but I did think that it would find a home somewhere," she said."It's got legs and it's not finished walking yet".Get in touchYour Voice

title: Rare zebra-striped bee sighting in West Country a 'huge surprise'
description: Figure caption, ByIsabella BeardSomersetA tiny zebra-striped bee, usually found along England's south and east coasts, has made an unexpected journey
body: Figure caption, ByIsabella BeardSomersetA tiny zebra-striped bee, usually found along England's south and east coasts, has made an unexpected journey to the West Country.The rare sea aster mining bee has been spotted at Steart Marshes in Somerset by naturalist Nigel Phillips, who said the find "was a huge surprise".The Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust said saltmarsh restoration work at the nature reserve had helped create the perfect home for the newcomer.The charity says the discovery shows how rare species and wildlife can thrive by restoring coastal habitats.Image source, Kit Houghton WWTImage caption, The species nests independently and relies on the saltmarsh plant called sea aster for foodThe reserve supports a wide variety of coastal wildflowers, including plenty of sea aster, which is thought to have finally attracted the bees to the Steart peninsula."There were lots of them and several colonial nest areas in the dry sandy ground," said Phillips."At the time I thought they were only found in salt marsh areas around the Thames estuary."Image source, Nick Turner WWTImage caption, Steart Marshes are an example of how restoring saltmarshes can boost wildlifeOf the 290 invertebrate species found in these habitats across the UK, 148 can only be found in saltmarshes.Site manager Bay Alys Laver said: "People usually associate saltmarshes with huge flocks of wading birds, geese and ducks, but there is so much life here that goes unnoticed."Spotting such a rare species here is a testament to the brilliant work our staff do in maintaining the reserve in concert with local graziers."I was so happy to hear that we have been found by our first sea aster mining bees."Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Somerset

title: World trekker Karl Bushby's final push home to Hull
description: He left 28 years ago, now after 36,000 miles Karl Bushby is almost homeImage source, Kevin Shoesmith/BBCImage caption, Karl Bushby bears down on Hull,
body: He left 28 years ago, now after 36,000 miles Karl Bushby is almost homeImage source, Kevin Shoesmith/BBCImage caption, Karl Bushby bears down on Hull, with his heavy duty gear trolley "The Beast" ByKevin ShoesmithEast Yorkshire and LincolnshireWith his journey almost complete, Karl Bushby reflects on adventures that have taken him across four continents, as well as strained relationships and how life as he knows it is about to change dramatically.Back in 1998, the former paratrooper, then aged 29, set off from Punta Arenas, Chile, to walk an unbroken path to his home city of Hull, without breaking two self-imposed rules: not to return to the UK until he had completed his journey, and not to use transport to advance.Now 57, he is embarking on his final few miles having hacked his way through the jungles of the Darién Gap, crossed the frozen Bering Strait and, just a few weeks ago, swum the English Channel.At the end, he will be met by his 36-year-old son Adam, a 12-year-old granddaughter whom he has never met, his father and brothers. His mother will be waiting at his childhood home that he left 28 years ago.Image source, Karl BushbyImage caption, Karl Bushby crossed the Bering Strait in 2006"We're definitely in terra incognita [unknown territory] right now, or pretty soon will be," says Bushby, as I join him in rural Lincolnshire."Right now, I'm comfortable because I'm doing what I do, but pretty soon that's going to screech to a halt."A bit like "The Beast", Bushby's heavy duty hardcart.Just a couple of miles into this leg, Bushby's handcart, which he uses to carry essential supplies, sustains a puncture.   "We haven't had one of these for a long time," he says. "This could be a pain. Damn."As I watched him attempt a hasty roadside repair, he flashed a grin before adding: "If it was raining, I'd probably be moaning a bit more.""The first few days that I was in Dover, it started raining. But we'd managed to just thread the needle as far as the weather was concerned. We had those perfect three days [for the swim]."Cars thunder past us.Bushby quips: "You guys know you drive on the wrong side of the road, right?" His use of the word "you" speaks of his disconnection from home.Figure caption, Watch: Karl Bushby's route from Punta Arenas, Chile, to his home city of HullBushby is well versed in overcoming physical barriers, such as a flat tyre.But is he prepared for what is to follow?"Everything that I am and everything that I know of me is going to go away," he says. "And that's going to be a problem. You're going to have the old identity crisis, because Karl is this [an adventurer] and has been for half his life. "I will have to figure out who I am again. What is the meaning to it all? How do I find that meaning and purpose? How do I fill that hole I'm suddenly going to find myself in?"Every fibre of my being, every day, has been what I'm doing right now. It has been the mission. "I think the old adage goes... the only thing worse than a man who can't fulfil his dreams is a man who's fulfilled his dreams... because then what?"Image source, Kevin Shoesmith/BBCImage caption, Bushby makes a roadside repair after his handcart sustains a puncture in LincolnshireAngela Maxwell, an American long-distance walker, joined him for the walk from Dover, where he landed after swimming the Channel."I think Karl might be surprised how much he'll miss the road," she says. "We joke sometimes that Karl doesn't love walking. But he loves the mission. He loves the passion, the purpose."Image source, Karl BushbyImage caption, Bushby emerges from the English Channel near DoverBushby has been surprised by the interest his return to the UK has stoked."It's been almost overwhelming. The amount of people that have recognised me along the way. It's cool. It gets a bit weird at times when people get really, really excited, and I just can't work out why. From my perspective, it just seems a little strange. "I'm some guy who's just walking."A car pulls into a lay-by and the driver asks if he is the Karl Bushby. The men pose for a selfie.Bushby has consistently denied this is a spiritual undertaking; a journey of discovery. But does he think the global interest in his story stems from an inner wanderlust present in many of us, but acted upon by few? "I think that's it," he says."I've lived a million men's dreams. A lot of people would love to walk away from home and just keep going."Bushby says his "opportunity to walk" came following the end of his marriage, with his wife returning to Northern Ireland with their son.Image source, Karl BushbyImage caption, Bushby, pictured centre, at the start of his 12-year Parachute Regiment careerThe reality of life on the road is not as rosy as it might first appear, it seems."I'm dealing with the day-to-day stuff - punctures, just trying to find a place where you can wash your underwear. That's my life. That's the mundane stuff, walking in the rain, it's never-ending kilometres."It's not as glorious as it looks."Bushby says he has only spent about 15 of the 28 years walking, often retreating to Mexico, where costs are low, between stints. The remainder of the time has been spent applying for visas and "dealing with geopolitics", he says. Travel restrictions during the Covid-19 pandemic also resulted in delays.Under the rules he set for his journey, Bushby could not return to the UK to meet his family.On rare occasions, he met his son and parents, who are divorced, in other countries. "Family is family, right?" says Bushby."They're always going to be there. But there will be strain. There will be distance. So much so that you've grown apart to some degree. You don't really know each other anymore. "As far as a love life goes, standby. You're going to take a kick in the nuts. It's not going to work out for you."Image source, Karl BushbyImage caption, He set off from Chile on 1 November 1998Soon after arriving in Dover, he tasted fish, chips and mushy peas for the first time in almost three decades. He said nowhere else in the world does the dish quite like the Brits.But venturing beyond the superficial, he appears not to have missed the UK."I've had the whole world to play with, so I've been distracted by many shiny things."Bushby believes he has not aged conventionally."I'm older, but I don't feel that old. I still feel way too young for my age, mentally. I still identify with that guy from the Americas way back when."With a twinkle in his eye, he adds: "I have still got that sense of adventure."His journey has also enabled him to meet many people."I personally have met the very best of humanity, and that's been a very uplifting thing. It's reaffirmed my belief and faith in humanity. The kindness of strangers made it all come together. "I couldn't have done it without the world."Before sponsors and a book deal, Bushby claims he was a "penniless backpacker" who relied on donations and even food discarded on roadsides to survive.Image source, Kevin Shoesmith/BBCImage caption, Bushby's mother, Angela, will be waiting for him at the gate to the home where she raised him He has advice for others pondering an adventure."Take any given opportunity. You can do a lot more than you ever imagined. A little bit of self-confidence will take you an awful long way. You're not going to achieve anything by not doing anything."What advice would he give to a young Bushby about to set off for Chile?"He doesn't want to hear it. You don't tell him anything. Just grin at him and let him be."Listen to highlights from Hull and East Yorkshire or Lincolnshire on BBC Sounds, watch the latest episode of Look North.Download the BBC News app from the App Store, external for iPhone and iPad or Google Play, external for Android devices

title: 'The necktie is dead': How US midterm candidates are dressing for votes
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByNardine SaadUS reporterAs Americans prepare to vote in the US midterm elections, candidates with their eye on Congress are
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByNardine SaadUS reporterAs Americans prepare to vote in the US midterm elections, candidates with their eye on Congress are not just competing on policy.In our social media age, they're using their personal style to attract attention and project their message. Their clothing has become a measure of their authenticity and appeal."Politicians are dressing for two jobs at once: to look capable of holding office but to also look connected to the people they want to represent," said Joe Zee, a celebrity fashion stylist.From Alaska to Texas, here is a look at how some candidates have been standing out on the campaign trail.Dressing like their stateSome candidates, like Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, who represents Washington's 3rd Congressional District, are embracing a relaxed, outdoorsy image.The former car repair shop owner is up for re-election on a platform focused on support for small businesses and working families, after capturing a Republican-held seat in her state in 2022. She favours low fuss, low-key work jackets, flannel shirts, jeans and practical footwear.Robert Ordway, conservative public policy adviser and former owner of Capitol Hill Clothiers, says Gluesenkamp Perez is probably the most "spot-on" when it comes to "authenticity and where you come from"."Also it really vibes with the Pacific Northwest, which has trees and forests and a little bit more of an outdoor vibe," he says.Her style also "shepherds a message championing the working class", says Tashira Halyard, an attorney, content creator, and public policy expert based in Washington DC.Image source, BBC NewsImage caption, Gluesenkamp Perez chooses a workwear-inspired wardrobeDemocratic lawmaker Mary Peltola, running for a Senate seat in the battleground state of Alaska, takes a similar approach.She made headlines for wearing traditional boots of the Yup'ik people while being sworn in as a congresswoman in 2022.During this election cycle, her rugged outdoor gear nods to her days working on a fishing boat on Alaska's Kuskokwim River and her "fish, family and freedom" campaign slogan.The flannels, puffer jackets and indigenous-inspired details seem designed to remind voters that Peltola is a native (and Native) Alaskan, says conservative author and journalist Bonnie Kristian.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Mary Peltola wore the traditional footwear of the Yup'ik people when she was sworn inPatriotism on their sleevesOther candidates, such as Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson of Iowa, have been opting for a bolder, patriotic image.While polished and conservative, her style of dress has included classic, arguably nostalgic touches, including denim and bandanas for more casual appearances.In a tight race against her Democratic opponent, Hinson has tried to separate herself from specific policy decisions made by the Trump administration but has still expressed loyalty to the president.She slipped into pumps with the American flag bedazzled across them at a primary election party in Iowa in June. The look, reminiscent of the style worn by Trump supporters at rallies, is quintessential American patriotism, according to Halyard."Ashley's American flag high heels, denim dress and bright red blouse worn with a bandana around her neck are classic Americana," she says."It's this idea that… I'm literally going to wear my patriotism on my sleeve."Image source, BBC NewsImage caption, Ashley Hinson's campaign style is inspired by the American flag Journalist Bonnie Kristian says there is "a strategic advantage" to Hinson's look, one in which she is "cultivating a visual identity that cannot possibly be misinterpreted" in an era where social media presence, if only for a split second, is crucial."Her denim dress, red bandana and sparkly American flag shoes all signal that she's a Republican wooing rural voters - and indeed she is."Tie off, cowboy boots onOnce a reliable Republican stronghold, Texas has become a battleground between top prosecutor Ken Paxton, 63, who was controversially endorsed by Trump over a longtime senator, and Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico, 37.On the campaign trail, both contenders have been making similar clothing choices, wearing relaxed blazers and cowboy boots.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Despite political differences, Talarico, left, and Paxton have similar wardrobes"The necktie is dead on the campaign trail in both parties," says Ordway."The younger man dresses up to look serious, and the older man dresses down to look like one of the guys."Fashion critic Friedman notes that Talarico's handcrafted Lucchese cowboy boots "are a very deliberate choice that allows him to speak to all different kinds of constituencies in Texas"."Those boots mean something that is very deeply rooted in Texas semiology," Friedman says, referring to the study of signs and their interpretations. "Former US President George W Bush wore Lucchese cowboy boots, so suddenly you're crossing all sorts of party lines and tapping into all sorts of different electoral groups with your shoes."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Former US president George W Bush was a fan of cowboy bootsMeanwhile, Paxton's style of dress has come under fire on more than one front. It has drawn the disapproval of Trump who has urged voters to focus on his record because it "speaks a lot louder than the suit he's wearing that doesn't look so great".The Republican candidate has also been criticised by his opponent for wearing a pricey watch and polo shirt from the luxury hotel chain Four Seasons as a debate about the high cost of living dominates the midterms."The criticism around his apparent luxury watch and Four Seasons polo raises another style-branded question: casual clothes don't necessarily communicate an ordinary lifestyle," says Zee, a stylist and faculty associate at Arizona State University's Fashion Institute of Design and Merchandising."A five-star resort-branded polo can carry luxury associations just as clearly as a suit. "The watch's identity and value were unconfirmed, but the perception illustrates how an accessory can complicate a candidate's message," he explains.Image source, Facebook/KenPaxtonTXImage caption, Paxton's watch and Four Seasons polo shirt drew criticismPersonal uniformsA uniform, if it reads naturally, is an incredibly effective tool, says Friedman, and a great way to be recognised across the country.It's an approach adopted by Republican Senator and former congresswoman for Tennessee's 7th congressional district, Marsha Blackburn, who is running for governor of her state.Senator Blackburn is often seen in structured jackets and skirts, sometimes with patterns. Ordway remembers that Blackburn "was extremely polished" whenever he spotted her in Capitol Hill while working there as a legislative director for a former Indiana senator."I always saw pearls on her," he says. "Since she's a veteran politician I think how she dresses in relation to how voters see her was probably decided many, many years ago."Image source, BBC NewsImage caption, Marsha Blackburn has been wearing a consistent style for decades"Her looks tend to be fairly timeless - we could imagine GOP women wearing many of them any time in the last three decades," Kristian adds.Meanwhile, Michigan Democratic candidate for US Senate Abdul El-Sayed, who is in a highly competitive race against a Trump-backed former congressman, has adopted a consistent look of black V-neck T-shirt and blue jeans.The left-wing political outsider, whose campaign slogan is "money out of politics, money in your pocket", refers to his outfit choices as "minimal look, maximal politics". The effect, says Ordway, is reminiscent of a start-up entrepreneur, designed to appeal to an urban, working-class electorate.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Abdul El-Sayed calls his outfit "minimal look, maximal politics"It also removes much of the "ceremony of a political appearance", Zee says."The suggestion is that attention should go to what he is saying. But the plain T-shirt remains an image choice. Looking un-styled can still be a deliberate form of branding."Trump, master of the imageImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Trump's suit and red tie is instantly recognisableFriedman notes that the master of this look in the US at the moment is Trump. His instantly recognisable power suit and red tie, ever-present in film and reality TV, were cultivated even before he moved into the White House."[Trump] doesn't just have his own merch, but he's got his own outfit, and now he's got all his cabinet wearing the same outfit, and half the Senate is wearing his outfit, and it becomes like a Pavlovian signifier," Friedman says."If they're wearing a navy suit, red tie, and white shirt, you're like, 'oh, that's a Trump person,'" she says.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Vice-President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent wear similar looksWhatever the outcome of the elections for Trump and his party, Friedman expects to see more politicians effectively branding themselves with their clothing when the 2028 general election rolls in."What we see is that so much of politics now is fought over social media and over TV, and that places a premium on visual messaging that is only going to become more important."

schema.headline: 'The necktie is dead': How US midterm candidates are dressing for votes

title: Lucy Harrison death: Mum told UK police have 'no authority' in US
description: The grand jury had decided there was insufficient evidence to bring criminal charges after Kris Harrison said the Glock handgun discharged accidentall
body: The grand jury had decided there was insufficient evidence to bring criminal charges after Kris Harrison said the Glock handgun discharged accidentally while he was showing it to his daughter.In February, a coroner in England concluded Lucy had been unlawfully killed, finding that her father's actions amounted to gross negligence manslaughter under UK law.Police in Texas have, however, said they would not reopen the investigation.Evans said the force was "ultimately constrained by legal, jurisdictional and practical realities that significantly limit what any police force in England and Wales can do in relation to a death that occurred in the United States," he said.Given the "unusual circumstances reported" of Lucy's death, a Senior Investigating Officer had been tasked with looking into the case. That officer appointed a Family Liaison Officer and sought information from the relevant United States law enforcement agencies.He said that despite the "clear jurisdictional limitations," the force's actions "reflected our recognition of the exceptional circumstances of the case and our commitment to providing whatever support and assistance was realistically available."The family had argued that as Kris Harrison is a British citizen, a mechanism exists under certain circumstances, where those from the United Kingdom who commit murder or manslaughter, can be prosecuted before British courts. In response, Evans said: "Even where jurisdiction may arguably exist in law, the practical ability to investigate and prosecute remains severely constrained when the suspect, witnesses, exhibits and evidential opportunities are all located overseas."No parent should have to endure the loss of a child in such tragic circumstances, and I fully appreciate that the passage of time does not diminish the family's need for answers or their determination to understand exactly what happened to Lucy," Evans added.Coates' lawyer Radd Seiger, has since said the family had "serious concerns" about the investigation and whether all the relevant evidence was properly gathered and considered.He added that further information, including a recent download from Lucy's mobile phone,  contained information which "we believe are relevant to the circumstances leading up to her death".Seiger said: "We are not asking Cheshire Constabulary to take over an American investigation or to determine what happened in Texas."Instead, he said, they were asking the force "to obtain and examine relevant evidence which has not yet been properly investigated"."The family have spent nearly two years trying to get answers about Lucy's death and justice for her. "They are not prepared to accept that the investigation is complete simply because the American authorities have decided not to take the matter further," he added.

schema.headline: Lucy Harrison death: Mum told UK police have 'no authority' in US

title: The Gloucestershire man who chooses to sleep with bedbugs
description: Figure caption, ByAlice BouverieReporting fromForest of DeanA scientist has chosen to sleep with bedbugs for the past five years - and says the bites
body: Figure caption, ByAlice BouverieReporting fromForest of DeanA scientist has chosen to sleep with bedbugs for the past five years - and says the bites "don't bother him at all".Entomologist Dr Richard Naylor breeds thousands of bedbugs to test pest control products from all over the world and allows himself to be the test subject.On a "feeding day", which happens around twice a week, he straps some of his 50-60,000 bugs to his arm and gets on with his work. He then sleeps with them on nights when he needs to test out new devices or repellents. "I must have been bitten millions of times by now, so I stopped reacting a long time ago. I get a red patch on my arm after the bugs have fed, but it disappears after about half an hour," he said. Naylor explained that he needed to sleep with the bugs to test if new sprays and repellents worked. "If there is no-one sleeping in a bed, the bedbugs just sleep, they just go on standby. And so I can't test anything in the test bedrooms without there being a host in there," he added.Naylor runs a not-for-profit called the Bed Bug Foundation and has a research laboratory set up in a self-contained two-bedroom suite in his garden in the Forest of Dean, Gloucestershire.He breeds the bugs and sends them all over the world, often to canine detection teams who help hotels spot infestations. Naylor also uses the insects to help businesses test products before they come to market.Bedbugs have become resistant to modern insecticide sprays, which makes them very difficult to kill and having an infestation can have long-lasting effects, according to Naylor. Image caption, Richard Naylor feeds around 20,000 bedbugs on his arm every three to four days"I don't know of any other pest that has the same level of emotional and psychological impact on people. "It can leave people with lasting PTSD-type symptoms," he added. Naylor said it could be difficult to deal with infestations and he advised anyone who suspected they had one to contact a professional. "A key sign you have bedbugs is the inky black spots the bugs leave behind, often in the shape of an x."They don't hide in the bedding, they want to hide nearby in a little dark crevice. It would probably be somewhere down the back of the bed or around zips and the piping around the edge of a mattress," he said. The Bed Bug Foundation gives the following advice to anyone who suspects they may have bad bugs:Declutter around the bed (helps you to spot bedbugs that try to run away)Remove bedding and other soft furnishings and put in bin bags for washingInspect the mattress and bed frame, especially near the head of the bedUse silica dust and vacuum thoroughlyFit bed isolation devices to stop the bedbugs coming backImage caption, Bedbugs mostly sleep during the day and are active at night when they sense a host nearbyAde Williams, lead pharmacist at Bedminster Pharmacy in Bristol, said bedbug bites tended to be clustered in a group, or be spread out in a line."Outside of the immense discomfort they cause by itching, they don't usually carry any health risks", he said. However, Williams advised people to try not to itch bites as they could become infected, and said antihistamine tablets and emollient creams could help.The NHS says a severe allergic reaction to bedbugs is possible, external but rare.It advises putting something cool, like a clean, damp cloth, on the affected area to help with the itching and any swelling and to keep the affected area clean.Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: The Gloucestershire man who chooses to sleep with bedbugs

title: Chelsea v Man Utd player ratings: Rogers and Palmer make the difference - how did Martinez rate?

body: Mike Penders: The Belgian goalkeeper remains under pressure after his mistake against Tottenham last week, but he was steady here and made several comfortable saves. 7Josh Acheampong: The young defender looked shaky early on but recovered well, making a fantastic block from a Bruno Fernandes volley and improving as the game went on. 6Wesley Fofana: The Frenchman made a brilliant block from one of Amad Diallo's shots but was twice at fault as the winger broke clear on the counter-attack. His header also struck the post after taking a deflection off Moises Caicedo in a chaotic display. Fofana also won the second-half penalty. 5Levi Colwill: The England defender was part of an overall poor defensive display but did not make any obvious errors himself. 6Marco Palestra: The Italian made some good recovery runs on his first start for Chelsea but was also part of a below-par defensive display from an organisational perspective. 7Moises Caicedo: Influential presence in a scrappy midfield battle, helping Chelsea compete physically in the centre of the pitch. 6Romeo Lavia: Often the player who helped Chelsea play through United's pressure, sparking several counter-attacks with intelligent passing. Won the ball for Chelsea's opener. 7Pedro Neto: Arguably Chelsea's most dangerous attacker but finishing let him down, with one effort saved and another fired well wide in the first half. 6Cole Palmer: A quiet game by his standards and unconvincingly scored a second-half penalty. Aside from that, he attempted an ambitious effort from inside his own half and gifted United one of their major chances. 6Estevao Willian: Lost possession with his first touch but recovered impressively. Looked lively throughout, having a couple of dangerous-looking shots on goal and two that he scored but were ruled out for offside. His set-pieces were also of consistent high quality. 8Morgan Rogers: A surprisingly anonymous start and struggled in the number nine position until he was given the chance to run at United's defence, scoring with a sublime dink in the 50th minute. 8Subs:Pep Chavarria (on 71, Palestra): Game was already won when he entered. 6Malo Gusto (on 86, Pedro Neto)Valentin Barco (on 86, Estevao Willian)Danny Welbeck (on 86, Moises Caicedo)Geovany Quenda on 90, Cole Palmer)Senne Lammens: Alive to Palmer's attempt to catch him out with a quickly taken free-kick. Was lucky to get away with a poor save early on, thanks to offside flag. Solid after that. No chance with Rogers goal. 7Leny Yoro: Speed essential to deal with Chelsea counter-attacks but sometimes ran out of position. 7Harry Maguire: Authoritative presence at heart of defence for most part but yet again unable to stop gap opening up for Rogers to score. 7Lisandro Martinez: Did OK and looked good - until Chelsea scored. Then gave penalty away and red-carded for ridiculous moment of recklessness. 3Diogo Dalot: Played out of position again at left-back and Estevao threatened down his side, but Dalot stuck to his task gamely. 6Andrey Santos: So close to a memorable goal against his old club. Crucial intervention to deny Moises Caicedo a clear sight at goal at the other end. Difficult second half. 5Carlos Baleba: Was having his best game in a United shirt so far and tried to prod the visitors forward. But impetuous tackle in midfield proved extremely costly as Rogers ran through to score. 5Amad Diallo: Looked sharp. Tested Mike Penders from long range and also at his near post. Fofana blocked another goal-bound effort. Should have scored before half-time. 7Bruno Fernandes: Returned as captain and should have put the visitors ahead when Mbeumo picked him out. Nearly set up Mbeumo. Better but not brilliant. 6Matheus Cunha: Most impact of any recent game. Linked well with the visitors' attack but didn't threaten a goal. 6Bryan Mbeumo: Set up a chance for Fernandes, then nearly reached a far-post cross from his captain. Gave Chelsea a problem but couldn't get last bit right. 6Subs:Kobbie Mainoo (on 58, Baleba): Not on long enough to make an impact before Martinez red. After that it was damage limitation. 6Ayden Heaven (on 66, Andrey Santos): Time for a regular start? 5Mason Mount (on 66, Cunha): Usual abuse from the home fans and nothing to answer it with. 5Joshua Zirkzee (on 77, Amad): 5
